objectives: Use a stack to check that brackets match.

Evaluate a postfix expression with a stack

screens.title: Undo
screens.prose: A spreadsheet keeps your edits on a pile, newest on top. You set a quantity, then a price, then deleted a row. Now you press Undo twice.

state.caption: The first edit is at the bottom, the newest on top

screens.question: Drag the edits that Undo removes into Undone.

hints.text: Which edit did you make most recently?
This is the newest edit, so the first Undo removes it.
The first Undo removes the row deletion. The second removes whatever is now on top: the price edit.

feedback.correct: Undo removed the newest edit, then the next newest.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each Undo removes the edit on top of the pile.

byKey.e1: You undid the first edit you made. Undo removes the newest edit still on the pile, never the bottom one.
byKey.e2: Undo ran twice. Once the row deletion is gone, the price edit is on top, so it goes next.
byKey.e3: The row deletion was your last edit, so the first Undo removes it.

explain.text: The first Undo took the row deletion, your newest edit. The second took the price edit, then on top. A pile like this is a **stack**: last in, first out.

canvas.caption: The quantity edit went in first and comes out last

screens.title: A list is a stack
screens.prose:
In Python a plain list is a stack. `append` puts a value on top and `pop()` takes the top value off.

```python
s = []
s.append("A")
s.append("B")
s.pop()
s.append("C")
s.append("D")
s.pop()
```
screens.question: Drag each value to where it ends up: still in `s`, or popped.

hints.text: What is on top of `s` when the first `pop()` runs?
B was pushed just before the first `pop()`.
The first `pop()` takes B. Then C and D go on, and the second `pop()` takes D. A and C stay.

feedback.correct: `s` ends as `['A', 'C']`; B and D were popped.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each `pop()` takes whatever was pushed most recently and is still there.

byKey.a: A went in first and nothing ever took it off. Each `pop()` took the value on top at that moment.
byKey.b: The first `pop()` ran right after B was pushed, so B was on top and came off.
byKey.c: C was pushed after B came off. The last `pop()` took D, which sat above C.
byKey.d: D was pushed last, so the final `pop()` took D.

explain.text: The first `pop()` took B, the newest value then. The second took D, not A. So `s` is `['A', 'C']`, and `s[-1]` reads the top, C.

canvas.caption: `s == ['A', 'C']`: the end of the list is the top

screens.title: Stepping through brackets
screens.prose: Undo always takes the newest edit. A closing bracket works the same way: it closes the most recent opener still open. So we read left to right and keep the openers on a stack.
screens.question: Step through `{[()]}`, one character at a time.

hints.text: Is the next character an opener or a closer?
A closer can see only the top of the stack.
Push `{`, `[` and `(`. Then each closer pops the top, which is its partner every time. Finish by checking the stack is empty.

feedback.correct: Every closer popped its partner, and nothing was left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Push each opener. Each closer pops the top and compares.

explain.text: `)` met `(`, `]` met `[` and `}` met `{`, each the top at that moment. Then the input ran out with the stack empty. Both facts together make the string balanced.

screens.title: Crossed brackets
screens.prose: In `([)]` every bracket has a partner of its own kind: two round and two square. Counting says it is fine. Run the stack on it instead.
screens.question: Step through `([)]` until you can give an answer.

ops.label: Pop the top and compare
ops.why: An opener has nothing to close yet. Push it so it can wait for its closer.

ops.label: Pop the top and compare
ops.why: An opener has nothing to close yet. Push it so it can wait for its closer.

ops.label: Reach under `[` and match `(`
ops.why: A stack shows only its top. Reaching under `[` would close `(` while `[` is still open inside it.

ops.label: Push `)`
ops.why: A closer is never pushed. It has to close the opener on top, so pop and compare.

ops.label: Carry on with `]`
ops.why: `)` cannot close `[`. One failed match is enough to answer: unbalanced.

canvas.caption: `)` arrived while `[` was the open bracket on top

hints.text: After `(` and `[`, which opener is on top?
`)` needs `(` on top. Is it there?
Push `(` and `[`. Then `)` pops `[`, which is not its partner, so the answer is unbalanced.

feedback.correct: `)` popped `[`: a mismatch, so `([)]` is unbalanced.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A closer pops the top and compares; it cannot reach under it.

explain.text: Counting would pass `([)]`: one pair of each kind. The stack catches the crossing, because `[` was on top when `)` arrived. Brackets must close in the reverse of the order they opened.

screens.title: The edge cases
screens.prose: A string is balanced when two things hold. Every closer finds its partner on top of the stack. And the stack is empty when the input runs out.
screens.question: Tap every input that is balanced.

hints.text: For each input, does any closer find the wrong top, or an empty stack?
This input has no brackets at all. Is anything unmatched?
`(()` leaves a `(` behind. `)(` and `]` start with a closer on an empty stack. The other three pass both checks.

feedback.correct: The empty string, `()[]{}` and `{[]}` are balanced.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check both conditions for each input: a matching top for every closer, and an empty stack at the end.

byKey.l1: The empty string has no brackets, so nothing is unmatched and the stack ends empty. It is balanced.
byKey.l2: `()[]{}` closes each pair straight away, and the stack ends empty. It is balanced.
byKey.l3: `(()` leaves one `(` on the stack when the input runs out. Leftover openers mean unbalanced.
byKey.l4: `)(` starts with a closer while the stack is empty, so there is nothing for it to close.
byKey.l5: `{[]}` nests one pair inside another, and each closer finds its partner on top. It is balanced.
byKey.l6: A lone `]` has nothing open to close. The stack is empty when it arrives.

explain.text: `(()` fails at the end: one opener is left. `)(` and `]` fail at once: a closer meets an empty stack. The empty string passes both checks, so it is balanced.

screens.title: Write the check
screens.prose: Now write it. The dictionary `pairs` maps each closer to its opener, so `pairs[")"]` is `"("`.
screens.question: Write `is_balanced(s)`: return `True` when every bracket in `s` is matched and properly nested.

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests, including the empty string, a lone closer and leftover openers. Characters that are not brackets are ignored.

hints.text: Push each opener. What must a closer find on top?
A lone closer finds the stack empty. Check that before you pop.
In the loop: append an opener. For a closer, `if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]: return False`. After the loop, `return not stack`.

feedback.correct: Your stack catches crossings, lone closers and leftover openers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 is the empty string, which is balanced. With nothing pushed, `return not stack` gives `True`.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is a lone `)`. Check `not stack` before you pop, or `pop()` raises `IndexError`.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 leaves three openers on the stack. End with `return not stack`, not `return True`.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has letters between the brackets. Skip any character that is neither an opener nor a closer.

explain.text: `not stack` comes first, so `pop()` never runs on an empty list. `return not stack` turns leftover openers into `False`. Each character is pushed or popped once, so the check is $O(n)$.

screens.title: Two bugs at the edges
screens.question: Which change fixes both calls?

options.text: `elif not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:` and `return not stack`
`elif stack.pop() != pairs[ch] or not stack:` and `return not stack`
options.why: You put `not stack` second. `or` runs left to right, so `pop()` still runs on the empty list and raises.

options.text: Wrap the loop in `try` with `except IndexError: return False`
options.why: That rescues the lone `)`, but `"(("` never raises: it reaches `return True` with two openers left.

options.text: Change only the last line to `return not stack`
options.why: That fixes `"(("`, but `")"` still calls `pop()` on an empty list and raises `IndexError`.

hints.text: Which call fails while reading, and which one fails at the end?
This line pops before it checks anything.
Guard the pop with `not stack` first, so `or` skips the pop on an empty stack. Then return `not stack` so leftovers count.

feedback.correct: Check the stack before popping, and again at the end.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. One fix has to stop the empty pop; the other has to catch leftover openers.

byKey.b: You put `not stack` after the pop. `or` evaluates left to right, so the pop still runs first and raises.
byKey.c: You caught the `IndexError`, but `"(("` raises nothing. It still returns `True` with openers left over.
byKey.d: You fixed the end of the loop only. A lone `)` still pops an empty list.

explain.text: `pop()` on an empty list raises `IndexError`, so test `not stack` first: `or` then skips the pop. `return True` ignored the two openers left by `"(("`. `return not stack` counts them.

screens.title: Postfix
screens.prose: In postfix notation each operator follows its two operands, so `3 4 +` means 3 + 4. A stack evaluates it. Push each number. An operator pops two numbers, combines them and pushes the result.
screens.question: What does `5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 -` evaluate to?

hints.text: Push 5, 1 and 2. What does the first `+` pop?
After `1 2 +` the stack is `[5, 3]`.
`4 *` gives 12, so the stack is `[5, 12]`. `+` gives 17. Then `3 -` pops 3 and 17 and pushes 17 − 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the stack on paper and update it at every token.

byKey.swapped: You computed 3 − 17. The first pop is the right operand: `b = pop()`, then `a = pop()`, then push `a - b`.
byKey.no-last: 17 is the value before the last two tokens. `3 -` still has to subtract 3.

explain.text: The stack ran `[5, 3]`, `[5, 12]`, `[17]`, then `[14]`. Each operator pops the right operand first, then the left one. For `-` and `/` that order matters.

screens.title: Write the evaluator
screens.prose: Tokens arrive as strings, such as `"12"`, `"-3"` or `"*"`. Turn each number into a `float`. The operators are `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`.
screens.question: Write `eval_postfix(tokens)`: return the value of a valid postfix expression.

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. Answers are compared with `==`, and `8.0 == 8` is `True`. Test 7 has a negative number, `"-3"`.

hints.text: Is the token an operator or a number?
For `10 2 -`, the first pop gives 2, the right operand.
For an operator: `b = stack.pop()`, `a = stack.pop()`, then push `a + b`, `a - b`, `a * b` or `a / b`. Otherwise push `float(tok)`.

feedback.correct: Numbers are pushed, operators pop two, and the result goes back on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 is `10 2 -`, which is 8. You computed 2 − 10: pop `b` first, then `a`, and push `a - b`.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has the token `"-3"`. Compare the whole token with each operator, as in `tok in ("+", "-", "*", "/")`, so `"-3"` counts as a number.

explain.text: The order of the two pops is the whole difficulty: `b` is popped first because it was pushed last. `"-3"` is a number, so compare whole tokens, not first characters. Each token costs $O(1)$, so the evaluator is $O(n)$.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
Every screen used one rule: the last item in is the first out.

```python
stack.append(x)    # push, O(1)
if stack:
    top = stack.pop()  # pop, O(1)
```

Python runs function calls on a stack too. A call waits on the **call stack** until the calls it made return (`algo-think`, lesson 6).
screens.question: `main` calls `price`, which calls `discount`. Which function returns first?

options.why: `main` started first, so it sits at the bottom of the call stack and finishes last.
`price` is waiting for `discount`, which is above it on the call stack.

feedback.correct: `discount` was called last, so it returns first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which call went onto the call stack last?

explain.text: Each call is pushed when it starts and popped when it returns. `discount` is on top, so it returns first; `main` went in first and comes out last. A `RecursionError` is this stack growing too tall.

screens.title: A broken formula
screens.prose: A risk sheet stores pricing formulas as text, and one bad bracket stops the whole sheet. The error message should point at the culprit. Keep **indices** on the stack instead of characters.

state.caption: Index 3 is the `(` after `max`, never closed

screens.question: Write `first_bad(s)`. It returns the index of the first closer with no partner on top. Failing that, it returns the index of the earliest opener left open, else −1.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests, including the empty formula, a lone opener and a lone closer.

hints.text: With indices on the stack, how do you read the opener's character?
Here every closer is matched, but one opener is left. Which index is at the bottom of the stack?
Use `for i, ch in enumerate(s)`, push `i` for an opener, and compare `s[stack.pop()]` with `pairs[ch]`. A failed closer returns `i`. At the end return `stack[0]` if anything is left, else −1.

feedback.correct: Your message points at the exact bracket that breaks the formula.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 leaves one opener, at index 3. Return the bottom of the stack, `stack[0]`, when openers are left.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has an extra `)` at index 13. Return its index when the stack is empty.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 is `((x)`. The inner pair closes, and the earliest opener still open is at index 0, the bottom of the stack.

explain.text: Indices tell you where each opener sits, and `s[i]` still gives its character. A closer that fails reports its own index. Left-over openers sit on the stack in reading order, so the earliest is `stack[0]`.

ideas: A stack gives items back in reverse order: last in, first out. A Python list is one, with `append` and `pop()` both $O(1)$.
Brackets match when each closer finds its partner on top of a stack of openers. The stack must also end empty.
Postfix expressions, undo history and the call stack all run on the same rule.

formula.name: Bracket check
formula.note: After the loop, `return not stack`: openers left over mean unbalanced.

summary.trap: `pop()` on an empty list raises `IndexError`, and `return True` forgets leftover openers. Check `not stack` before the pop and again at the end.

quiz.prose:
```python
s = []
for x in [3, 1, 4]:
    s.append(x)
s.pop()
s.append(5)
print(s)
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You removed 3, the first value in. `pop()` takes the last value, 4.
You skipped the `pop()`. It removes 4 before 5 goes on.
`append` adds at the end of the list, which is the top of the stack, not the front.

feedback.correct: `pop()` took 4, the last value in, and 5 went on top.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which value is on top when `pop()` runs?

explain.text: After the loop `s` is `[3, 1, 4]`, with 4 on top. `pop()` removes 4 and `append(5)` puts 5 on top. So `s` is `[3, 1, 5]`.

quiz.prose: Evaluate the postfix expression `2 3 4 * +` with a stack.
quiz.question: What is its value?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Push 2, 3 and 4, then apply each operator to the top two values.

byKey.left-to-right: You worked left to right, as (2 + 3) × 4. In postfix, `*` comes first here: it pops 4 and 3.

explain.text: The stack is `[2, 3, 4]` when `*` arrives. It pops 4 and 3 and pushes 12. Then `+` pops 12 and 2 and pushes 14.

quiz.prose: `is_balanced` is the finished version from the lesson.
quiz.question: Which call returns `True`?

options.why: The counts match, but `}` arrives while `(` is on top. The pairs cross.
Every closer matches, but one `(` is still on the stack at the end.
`)` arrives first, with nothing on the stack to close.

feedback.correct: `{[]()}` closes each pair in reverse order of opening.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step a stack through each string.

explain.text: In `{[]()}` the `[]` and `()` pairs each close at once, then `}` meets `{`. The stack ends empty, so it is balanced. The other three cross, leave an opener, or start with a closer.

quiz.prose: An editor keeps its undo history in a Python list with millions of entries.
quiz.question: Which pair of operations keeps each edit and each Undo $O(1)$?

options.why: Both work at the front, and every other entry has to shift one place. That is $O(n)$ each.
`pop(0)` removes the oldest edit, so Undo would undo the wrong thing. It also shifts every entry.

feedback.correct: The end of a list is the cheap end, so it is the top.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which end of a list can change without moving the rest?

explain.text: A list stores its values side by side from index 0. Adding or removing at the end moves nothing else, so `append` and `pop()` are $O(1)$. Working at the front shifts every value.

quiz.prose: A message format nests groups with start and end tags, such as `<order><leg></leg></order>`. A feed sends `<order><leg></order></leg>`.
quiz.question: How should a parser catch this?

options.text: Push each start tag's name; an end tag must match the name on top
Count start and end tags; reject if the counts differ
options.why: You counted tags. Here both counts are two, yet `</order>` closes while `<leg>` is still open.

options.text: Check that each end tag's name appeared earlier
options.why: Both names appeared earlier. The problem is the order they close in.

options.text: Match each end tag with the first start tag
options.why: That pairs `</order>` with `<order>` and passes. The most recent open tag is `<leg>`.

feedback.correct: Tags nest like brackets, so a stack of names checks them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which open tag must the first end tag close?

explain.text: When `</order>` arrives, the open tag on top of the stack is `<leg>`, so the message is malformed. Counting cannot see this, just as it could not see `([)]`.
